summary:
Matthew opens with a genealogy arranged in three deliberate sets of fourteen generations, tracing Jesus' lineage from Abraham through David to Joseph, the husband of Mary. This gospel is written primarily for a Jewish audience, and from its first verse it argues that Jesus is the long-awaited Messiah of Israel, the rightful heir to David's throne, the fulfillment of centuries of prophecy. Matthew quotes the Hebrew scriptures more than any other gospel writer, repeatedly using the phrase "this was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet."

The gospel is organized around five major blocks of teaching, each ending with a variation of "when Jesus had finished saying these things" — an architecture many readers have seen as an echo of the five books of Moses, with Jesus as a new and greater lawgiver. The first block is the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5-7). Blessed are the poor in spirit. Turn the other cheek. Love your enemies. Do not worry about tomorrow. Again and again Jesus cites what earlier generations were told — "you have heard that it was said" — and answers, "But I tell you": not only murder but anger, not only adultery but the lustful look. The other discourses address mission (chapter 10), parables of the kingdom (chapter 13), life in the community of believers (chapter 18), and the end of the age (chapters 24-25).

Matthew's Jesus is authoritative and commanding. He heals lepers, calms a storm, casts out demons, and feeds thousands — but always with an eye toward what these acts reveal about the kingdom breaking into the present world. The parables are vivid and unsettling: wheat and weeds growing together until harvest, a pearl worth selling everything to possess, a king who forgives a servant a debt of ten thousand talents — far more than a laborer could earn in a lifetime — only to watch him choke a fellow servant over a hundred denarii, a few months' wages. The kingdom of heaven, Matthew insists, is both already here and not yet fully realized, and it consistently overturns human expectations about who is in and who is out.

The conflict with the religious establishment builds steadily. Chapter 23 contains the most blistering speech in the gospel — seven woes against the scribes and Pharisees, calling them whitewashed tombs, beautiful on the outside but full of death within. It is an indictment in the style of Israel's own prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Amos pronounced woes like these against their own nation from within. The tension leads inevitably to the cross. Judas betrays Jesus for thirty pieces of silver. Peter denies him three times. Pilate washes his hands. Jesus is crucified between two criminals, and at his death the temple curtain tears from top to bottom, the earth quakes, rocks split, and tombs break open — the earthquake and the opened tombs are details only Matthew records.

The resurrection in Matthew is dramatic. An earthquake. An angel whose appearance is like lightning rolls back the stone and sits on it while the guards collapse like dead men. The women run from the tomb with fear and great joy. And the gospel ends on a mountain in Galilee, where the risen Jesus delivers the Great Commission: "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations." The book that began with a Jewish genealogy ends with a universal mandate. The Messiah of Israel turns out to be the Lord of everything.

Matthew brackets his gospel with a single promise. The child of the opening chapter is named Immanuel — "God with us" (1:23) — and the risen Jesus' final words on the mountain are "And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age" (28:20). Everything between those two verses unfolds under the same claim: in Jesus, God is present with his people.
